analysis.one_liner: Bars federal surveillance of Americans under FISA and Executive Order 12333.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the Senate with no cosponsors, referred to the Judiciary Committee, and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act so that federal officers could no longer seek, and the secret FISA court could no longer issue, orders to electronically surveil a United States person, physically search their property, collect their phone records, or seize their records. It would also ban the FBI and other agencies from searching data collected under Section 702 — foreign surveillance that sweeps in Americans' communications — using terms tied to an American. Finally, it would bar the government from using information about Americans gathered under Executive Order 12333 in any investigation or court case, except when the targeted person themselves wants to use it.
analysis.who_benefits: Every American would gain stronger Fourth Amendment-style protection: the government could no longer surveil a U.S. person under FISA's lower standards, could no longer run warrantless searches of Americans' communications in Section 702 data, and could no longer build criminal cases on information gathered through foreign-intelligence programs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary Americans' privacy and phone records

how_it_helps.text: The bill forbids federal officers from requesting, and the FISA court from issuing, orders for electronic surveillance, physical searches, pen registers, or production of records concerning a United States person under FISA [S2].

It prohibits any query of Section 702-collected information using search terms associated with a United States person, closing the 'backdoor search' loophole that lets the FBI search foreign surveillance data for Americans' communications [S2].

It bars the government from using information about a United States person acquired or derived from FISA surveillance, or from Executive Order 12333 intelligence collection, in any criminal, civil, or administrative proceeding or investigation [S2].

It makes statutory and court-authorized warrants the exclusive means for searching or collecting a U.S. person's communications or records, ending surveillance of Americans that currently happens under the executive order rather than a judge's warrant [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The intelligence community and federal law enforcement would lose surveillance tools they currently use against Americans, including warrantless backdoor searches of Section 702 data and use of foreign-program information in domestic cases. Genuine foreign targets who are U.S. persons or on U.S. soil would have to be pursued through normal warrants.

drawbacks.text: National security agencies and their supporters argue that FISA and Section 702 tools have been essential for catching terrorists, spies, and foreign hackers, and that a blanket ban on surveilling U.S. persons could leave dangerous gaps when an American is working with a foreign adversary. The bill itself acknowledges the stakes by carving out ordinary criminal warrants as the alternative channel [S2].

The complete ban on using FISA-derived information in any proceeding is broader than current law requires; critics argue courts already screen out unlawfully obtained evidence, and a total ban could hamper legitimate prosecutions that rest partly on foreign-intelligence information [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The privacy gains for ordinary Americans are substantial and concrete: no more warrantless backdoor searches of their communications and no more criminal cases built on foreign-program collection. The cost is real but narrower — investigators would have to use ordinary warrants to pursue Americans, which is slower in urgent counterintelligence cases but is the route the Fourth Amendment normally requires. The bill is aggressively written and would likely need exceptions to pass, but its core tradeoff is that the government needs a warrant to spy on an American.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced, and died there without a hearing or vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Rand Paul introduced S. 3372 on November 30, 2023; the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S1] [S4].
No senator signed on as a cosponsor [S3].
The bill received no further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The intelligence and law enforcement agencies keep their existing surveillance authorities over Americans, and nothing changed for anyone else. Because the bill never moved, no member of Congress had to take a public position on warrantless surveillance of U.S. persons.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, so the record shows no partisan bloc took a position; it never reached a vote [S3] [S4].

industries.industry: U.S. intelligence and law enforcement agencies (NSA, FBI, CIA)
industries.note: The bill strips their authority to surveil Americans under FISA and Executive Order 12333, bans backdoor searches of Section 702 data for U.S.-person information, and bars use of such information in domestic investigations. Their interest in keeping these tools runs directly against the privacy of ordinary Americans. This is a government interest rather than a private industry, but it is the concentrated interest the bill targets.

Providers currently receive FISA and pen-register orders for customer data; the bill would reduce compelled production of U.S. persons' records, though foreign-target requests would continue. The effect on their bottom line is small either way.
